title: 01  WHAT A FOURIER COEFFICIENT MEANS
steps: $x(t)=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}a_ke^{jk\omega_0t}$

A Fourier series does something surprisingly simple. It builds a periodic signal by adding a constant and oscillating pieces. Each index k tells us which harmonic we are dealing with. The coefficient a sub k tells us how much of that harmonic is present, and what its phase is.
$\omega_0=\frac{2\pi}{T},\qquad f_0=\frac{1}{T}$

Omega naught is the fundamental angular frequency. It is two pi divided by the period, in radians per second. The ordinary frequency is one over the period, in hertz. Keep those two units separate because an exam can switch between them.
$k=0\;\Rightarrow\;a_0\ \mathrm{is\ DC}$

At k equals zero, the exponential becomes one, so the coefficient is just a constant. That is the DC component, or the average level of the periodic signal. A nonzero a sub zero shifts the whole waveform vertically.
$k=\pm1,\pm2,\pm3,\ldots$

At plus or minus one, we have the fundamental frequency. At plus or minus two we have twice the fundamental. When the signal is real, coefficients at positive and negative indices appear as complex conjugate pairs. That fact will save us work.
Identify the tones before expanding anything.

Here is the habit to develop: before using Euler's formula, scan the given time-domain signal. Count the constant, cosine, and sine terms. Predict which indices can be nonzero. That makes the algebra a verification of your reasoning instead of a guessing process.

title: 02  F26 REVIEW QUESTION 2: START
steps: $x(t)=2+4\cos(\omega_0t-\pi/3)+2\sin(2\omega_0t)$

Let's use your professor's actual review question two. The signal contains a constant two, a cosine with amplitude four at omega naught, and a sine with amplitude two at two omega naught. We want the exponential Fourier series coefficients.
$\omega_0=2\pi(50)=100\pi\ \mathrm{rad/s}$

The question tells us the fundamental angular frequency is two pi times fifty. That means the ordinary fundamental frequency is fifty hertz. So each harmonic index corresponds to another multiple of fifty hertz.
$T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_0}=\frac{1}{50}=0.020\ \mathrm{s}$

Let's compute the period. Two pi divided by one hundred pi simplifies to one fiftieth of a second, or twenty milliseconds. Notice that later a five millisecond delay will be one quarter of this period.
$a_0,\ a_{\pm1},\ a_{\pm2}\quad\mathrm{may\ be\ nonzero}$

Without writing a single exponential, we can list the only possible nonzero positions. The constant produces k zero. The cosine produces plus and minus one. The sine produces plus and minus two. Every other index must be zero.
We can immediately write a sub zero equals two. Nothing else in this signal has nonzero average over a period. That settles the DC coefficient without an integral.
Why isn't the cosine one single coefficient?

This is an important conceptual check. A real cosine is made from two counter-rotating complex exponentials. One lives at positive frequency, and one at negative frequency. We need both coefficients to reconstruct the same real sinusoid.

title: 03  F26 QUESTION 2: COSINE PAIR
steps: $\cos\theta=\frac{e^{j\theta}+e^{-j\theta}}{2}$

Now recall Euler's cosine identity. A cosine splits into the sum of positive and negative complex exponentials, divided by two. That division is why a cosine amplitude of four becomes two in each frequency coefficient.
$4\cos(\omega_0t-\pi/3)$
Take only the cosine term for now, and leave the sine alone. This is the cleanest way to work: expand one sinusoid, identify its harmonic coefficients, and then proceed to the next.

Applying the identity, we get two exponentials. The first has positive j multiplying the entire angle. The second has negative j multiplying the entire angle. Every sign inside those parentheses matters.
$=2e^{-j\pi/3}e^{j\omega_0t}+2e^{j\pi/3}e^{-j\omega_0t}$

Separate the time-dependent part from the phase constant. When the negative sign distributes into negative pi over three, it becomes positive pi over three. This step is where sign mistakes often appear.

Now match these terms to the Fourier series form. The coefficient multiplying e to the plus j omega naught t is a sub one. The coefficient multiplying e to the minus j omega naught t is a sub negative one.

Their magnitudes are both two, and their phases are opposite. That conjugate symmetry is exactly what we expect for a real-valued signal. If your coefficients do not have this relationship, revisit your signs.

title: 04  F26 QUESTION 2: SINE PAIR
steps: $\sin\theta=\frac{e^{j\theta}-e^{-j\theta}}{2j}$

Sine looks similar to cosine, but now we subtract the negative-frequency exponential and divide by two j. Do not replace this with the cosine identity. A missing j changes the phase of your coefficients.
$2\sin(2\omega_0t)$
Take the original sine term, which has amplitude two and angular frequency two omega naught. The harmonic number will be plus or minus two, not plus or minus one.
$=\frac{e^{j2\omega_0t}-e^{-j2\omega_0t}}{j}$
The amplitude two cancels the two in the denominator of the sine identity. We are left with the difference of two exponentials divided by j.
$j^2=-1\quad\Rightarrow\quad\frac{1}{j}=-j$

Let's explicitly simplify one over j. Multiply numerator and denominator by j. That gives j over j squared, or j over negative one, which equals negative j. Memorizing this one result is useful, but knowing why makes you less likely to forget.
$2\sin(2\omega_0t)=-je^{j2\omega_0t}+je^{-j2\omega_0t}$
Distribute negative j into the first term and positive j into the second. Notice how the sine produces imaginary coefficients of opposite sign, as we should expect for a real sine.
So a sub two is negative j, and a sub negative two is positive j. Both have magnitude one. They are complex conjugates, even though the original sine had amplitude two.
Quick check: do both terms recreate a sine?

Add the two terms and factor out one over j. You recover the difference between the positive and negative exponentials, which is the original sine. This is an excellent ten-second check during the exam.

title: 05  F26 QUESTION 2: COMPLETE ANSWER
steps: Let's collect the results in one place. The DC value is two, and the first positive and negative harmonics have magnitude two and opposite phases.
The second harmonic pair has magnitude one, with opposite imaginary signs. The harmonic locations come from the frequencies, not from the amplitudes.
$a_k=0\quad\mathrm{for}\ |k|>2$
There are no additional sinusoidal terms in the input, so every other Fourier coefficient is zero. Do not add imaginary extra harmonics just because the summation symbol ranges over all integers.
When plotting magnitude, ignore phase for the moment. Plot a stem at zero of height two; stems at plus and minus one of height two; and stems at plus and minus two of height one.
What changes if the signal is delayed?

The next part introduces a time shift. Here is the key prediction before we calculate: a pure delay cannot change how much of each frequency is present. It can only change where each sinusoid is in its cycle.

title: 06  F26 QUESTION 2: TIME DELAY
steps: $y(t)=x(t-t_0),\qquad t_0=0.005\ \mathrm{s}$

The entire signal is delayed by five milliseconds. The question asks for the new coefficients b sub k, in terms of the original a sub k. We can use the Fourier series time-shift property instead of re-expanding every sine and cosine.
$b_k=a_ke^{-jk\omega_0t_0}$

A rightward time shift multiplies every coefficient by a complex phase factor. The exponent contains negative j, the harmonic index k, the fundamental angular frequency, and the time delay. The negative sign corresponds to a delay.

Substitute the known numbers. One hundred pi radians per second times zero point zero zero five seconds equals pi over two radians. This is a ninety-degree phase rotation for the fundamental harmonic.
$b_k=a_ke^{-jk\pi/2}$

Now insert pi over two into the time-shift expression. This compact result is sufficient for the question, because it expresses every new coefficient in terms of the old coefficient and the harmonic number.

For a concrete example, k equals one. Multiply the original first-harmonic coefficient by e to the negative j pi over two. Add the phases: negative pi over three minus pi over two gives negative five pi over six.
$|b_k|=|a_k|\quad\mathrm{for\ every}\ k$

The magnitude of any complex exponential e to the j theta is one. Therefore every coefficient keeps the same magnitude. A delay changes phase only. This is an important conceptual answer as well as an algebraic property.
A quarter-period delay is not a frequency change.

Remember the period is twenty milliseconds. A five millisecond delay is one quarter period. You should picture the same waveform moved right by one quarter of a cycle. The spectrum stays at the same harmonic frequencies.

title: 07  F19 EXAM QUESTION 1: FILTER
steps: $a_k=\frac{1}{3+k^2},\quad\omega_0=\pi/2$

Let's switch to a real Fall twenty nineteen exam question. Here the Fourier coefficients are already given, as one over three plus k squared. We don't need to derive them from a waveform. We need to determine what the filter keeps.
$T=\frac{2\pi}{\omega_0}=4\ \mathrm{s}$
First, identify the period. Omega naught is pi over two radians per second, so two pi divided by pi over two gives four seconds. This is a straightforward place to earn credit.
At k equals zero, the coefficient is one over three. Since DC is the zero-frequency component, this is also the average value of the signal.
$H(\omega)=1\quad\mathrm{for}\ |\omega|<0.6\pi$
The ideal low-pass filter passes frequencies strictly between negative zero point six pi and positive zero point six pi. Frequencies outside that interval are rejected.
$\omega_k=k\omega_0=k\pi/2$

Here is the crucial step. A Fourier series has discrete harmonic frequencies k times omega naught. We do not need to inspect every real number on the frequency axis. We only check the frequencies where harmonic stems exist.
$k=0:\ 0\qquad k=\pm1:\ \pm0.5\pi$
The zero harmonic is inside the passband. The positive and negative first harmonics are at plus and minus zero point five pi. Those are also inside zero point six pi, so all three survive.
$k=\pm2:\ \pm\pi\quad\mathrm{are\ blocked}$
At harmonic two, the angular frequency is pi, which is larger than zero point six pi in magnitude. Harmonics two and higher, both positive and negative, do not pass the filter.

title: 08  F19 FILTER: REBUILD THE OUTPUT
steps: $y(t)=\sum_k a_kH(k\omega_0)e^{jk\omega_0t}$

For a linear time-invariant filter, each Fourier coefficient gets multiplied by the frequency response at its harmonic frequency. Because the filter is either zero or one, we can simply delete the rejected terms.
$y(t)=\frac13+\frac14e^{j\pi t/2}+\frac14e^{-j\pi t/2}$
Only the constant and the plus-or-minus first harmonic survive. At k one and negative one, the coefficient is one over four. Put those three terms into the time-domain Fourier sum.
$e^{j\theta}+e^{-j\theta}=2\cos\theta$
Now combine the exponential pair using Euler's cosine identity in reverse. The sum of the positive and negative exponential equals two cosine of the same angle.
$y(t)=\frac13+\frac12\cos(\pi t/2)$
Multiplying the one-quarter by two gives one-half. The filtered output is one third plus one half cosine of pi t over two. Notice how the constant survived and the faster harmonics disappeared.
Exam shortcut: mark passed k-values first.

The fastest reliable method is: write the fundamental, evaluate a few harmonic frequencies, circle those inside the passband, and reconstruct only those terms. A convolution integral would be much more work here.

title: 09  F26 REVIEW QUESTION 4: TONE FILTER
steps: Now consider question four from the current review. The input consists of two cosine waves: one at one hundred hertz with amplitude two, and one at five hundred hertz with amplitude one.
$|f|<300\ \mathrm{Hz}\quad\mathrm{passes}$
The filter's cutoff is three hundred hertz. It is written using angular frequency in the problem, but dividing by two pi reveals that the passband is below three hundred hertz in magnitude.
$100<300\quad\Rightarrow\quad\mathrm{PASS}$
Compare the first frequency to the cutoff. One hundred is less than three hundred, so the entire one-hundred-hertz cosine is passed without attenuation by this ideal filter.
$500>300\quad\Rightarrow\quad\mathrm{REMOVE}$
The five-hundred-hertz cosine is above the cutoff, so it is removed. This is not a matter of subtracting frequencies or changing its amplitude slightly. The ideal response is zero there.

The output is simply the original one-hundred-hertz term. This question is an easy illustration of the central LTI fact: filtering changes the amplitudes and phases of existing frequencies according to H, rather than creating new frequencies.
$Y(\omega)=X(\omega)H(\omega)$

That is why multiplication in the frequency domain is so powerful. Each frequency component is handled independently. For a spectrum made of only two cosine tones, the multiplication is just two pass-or-block decisions.

title: 10  F26 Q4: TIME SCALING AND DELAY
steps: Part c changes the input signal before passing it through the same filter. Replacing t by two t compresses the waveform in time. A compressed oscillation completes its cycles twice as quickly.
Multiply every frequency by two. The hundred-hertz tone becomes two hundred hertz. The five-hundred-hertz tone becomes one thousand hertz. Importantly, the amplitudes remain two and one.
The two-hundred-hertz tone still lies below the three-hundred-hertz cutoff, so it passes. The one-thousand-hertz tone does not. Our output is a two-hundred-hertz cosine with amplitude two.

Part d instead delays the original signal by two point five milliseconds. A time delay does not change the frequency of either input tone. The low-pass filter still keeps only the hundred-hertz component.

Write the delayed version of the tone that passed. Since this is a time-invariant filter, delaying the input delays the output by the same amount. We do not need to recompute a new magnitude spectrum.
Distribute the factor of two pi times one hundred. The delay corresponds to a phase shift of pi over two radians at one hundred hertz. Note that the phase shift depends on frequency.
Cosine of theta minus pi over two equals sine of theta. So we can also express the output as two sine of two pi one hundred t. The magnitude spectrum has not changed; only its phase has.

title: 11  F26 Q3: INPUT SPECTRUM
steps: $x(t)=\frac{\sin(1000\pi t)}{t}$

The modulation problem looks harder, but we will divide it into smaller decisions. First identify the Fourier transform of the input. The signal is sine of one thousand pi t over t, and the question gives a matching transform pair.
$\frac{\sin(\omega_bt)}{\pi t}\ \longleftrightarrow\ 1\ \mathrm{inside}\ |\omega|<\omega_b$

The provided pair says sine of omega b t divided by pi t corresponds to a rectangular spectrum of height one, from negative omega b to positive omega b. Look very carefully at the pi in the denominator.
$x(t)=\pi\frac{\sin(1000\pi t)}{\pi t}$
Our actual signal has t in the denominator, not pi t. Multiply the standard expression by pi to match the given x. That means the spectrum height will also be multiplied by pi.
$X(\omega)=\pi\quad\mathrm{for}\ |\omega|<1000\pi$
So X of omega is a rectangle with height pi, extending from negative one thousand pi to positive one thousand pi radians per second. Outside that interval, it is zero.
$f=\frac{\omega}{2\pi}\quad\Rightarrow\quad |f|<500\ \mathrm{Hz}$

The review specifically asks for horizontal axes in hertz. Divide the angular frequency boundaries by two pi. One thousand pi divided by two pi is five hundred, so the rectangle spans minus five hundred to plus five hundred hertz.
Write both the width and the height.
A spectrum sketch is incomplete if you label only the frequency boundaries. Here the height is pi, not one. That factor matters later when the signal is multiplied by the squared carrier.

title: 11B  DRAW THE INPUT SPECTRUM
steps: $X(\omega)=\pi\ \mathrm{for}\ |f|<500\ \mathrm{Hz}$

Let's draw what we just calculated. Start at negative five hundred hertz and draw a vertical line up to height pi. Draw the top of the rectangle across to positive five hundred hertz, then return to the axis.
$\mathrm{height}=\pi,\qquad\mathrm{width}=1000\ \mathrm{Hz}$
Label the height pi and both edge frequencies. Remember the physical spectrum is even because the input is real and even, so it looks symmetric around zero.
$\mathrm{outside\ the\ rectangle:}\ X(\omega)=0$
Everywhere outside the rectangle the spectrum is zero. This wideband rectangle is not three separate impulses. It represents a continuum of frequencies; the impulses appear later for the carrier.
The next operation copies this rectangle.
Once you have this picture, multiplication by a cosine becomes a geometric operation. You make two smaller copies, shift one right and one left, and add them to the centered piece.

title: 12  F26 Q3: CARRIER AND SQUARE
steps: The carrier is cosine of two thousand pi t. Since the coefficient of t equals two pi times ordinary frequency, this is a one-thousand-hertz carrier. Be careful not to call it two thousand hertz.
$f_c=1000\ \mathrm{Hz}$
The carrier has positive and negative spectral impulses at plus and minus one thousand hertz. Under the continuous-time Fourier transform convention, each impulse has weight pi.

The transmitted and demodulated signal is multiplied by the carrier twice, so the multiplier is cosine squared. The square is not another regular cosine at the same frequency; we must apply a double-angle identity.
$\cos^2\theta=\frac12+\frac12\cos(2\theta)$
Use the power-reduction identity. This identity can also be derived from Euler's formulas, but writing it directly is faster here. It shows a DC contribution and a cosine at double frequency.
$q(t)=\frac12+\frac12\cos(4000\pi t)$
After substituting the angle, the squared carrier contains a constant one-half and a half-amplitude cosine at four thousand pi radians per second, which means two thousand hertz.
$Q(\omega)=\pi\delta(\omega)+\frac{\pi}{2}\delta(\omega-4000\pi)+\frac{\pi}{2}\delta(\omega+4000\pi)$

This is the spectrum of q. The constant half produces an impulse at zero with weight pi. The half-amplitude cosine produces impulses at positive and negative four thousand pi, each with weight pi over two.
Remember: c is at 1000 Hz; q has lines at 0 and 2000 Hz.

This distinction is an exam favorite. Squaring the carrier doubles the oscillatory frequency and introduces DC. The three impulse locations for the squared carrier are zero and plus or minus two thousand hertz.

title: 13  F26 Q3: THREE SPECTRAL COPIES
steps: $y(t)=x(t)q(t)$

The demodulated signal is the input multiplied by q, the squared carrier. In general, time-domain multiplication means convolution in the frequency domain. But because q is a sum of impulses, we can compute the answer using simple spectral shifts.
$y(t)=\frac12x(t)+\frac12x(t)\cos(4000\pi t)$
Substitute our squared-carrier identity directly into y of t. We obtain one-half of the original input plus another term where the input multiplies a cosine at two thousand hertz.
$\cos(4000\pi t)=\frac12e^{j4000\pi t}+\frac12e^{-j4000\pi t}$
Now expand the cosine into its positive and negative rotating complex exponentials. The two halves combine with the one-half outside to give one-quarter for each shifted copy.
$Y(\omega)=\frac12X(\omega)+\frac14X(\omega-4000\pi)+\frac14X(\omega+4000\pi)$

This is the full spectrum after the two carrier multiplications. One centered rectangle stays at zero with half its old height. Two additional rectangles appear shifted right and left by four thousand pi radians per second.
$\mathrm{center:}\ [-500,500]\ \mathrm{Hz},\ \mathrm{height}\ \pi/2$
The centered copy retains the original five-hundred-hertz edge on each side. Its height is half of pi, because the coefficient is one-half.

The shifted rectangles are centered at plus and minus two thousand hertz. Each has the same half-width of five hundred hertz. Therefore the right one extends from fifteen hundred to twenty-five hundred, and the left one from negative twenty-five hundred to negative fifteen hundred hertz.
$\mathrm{sideband\ heights}=\pi/4$

Because each shifted copy has coefficient one-quarter, its height is pi over four. Keeping the height and the frequency locations separate makes these spectrum sketches much easier to label correctly.

title: 13B  DRAW THE THREE COPIES
topic: THIS IS THE CENTRAL MODULATION PICTURE
steps: $Y=\frac12X+\frac14X_{\mathrm{right}}+\frac14X_{\mathrm{left}}$
Now turn the algebra into a drawing. Start with the original rectangle between negative and positive five hundred hertz, but make its height pi over two. That is the centered copy.
$\mathrm{right}\ \mathrm{band}:\ 1500\ \mathrm{to}\ 2500\ \mathrm{Hz}$
Next draw an equal-width rectangle centered at positive two thousand hertz. Its left edge is fifteen hundred and its right edge twenty-five hundred. Its height is pi over four.
$\mathrm{left}\ \mathrm{band}:\ -2500\ \mathrm{to}\ -1500\ \mathrm{Hz}$

Now mirror it on the negative side. Its center is negative two thousand hertz. Both sidebands are farther than one thousand hertz from the origin, so a low-pass filter with one-thousand-hertz cutoff can remove them.
Frequency shifts do not stretch the rectangles.

Each rectangle retains its original width of one thousand hertz. Modulation changes the center frequencies and amplitudes, not the width of each shifted copy. That distinction helps avoid incorrect spectral drawings.

title: 14  F26 Q3: IDEAL LOW-PASS RECOVERY
steps: $H(\omega)=1\quad\mathrm{for}\ |\omega|<2000\pi$

Now the signal passes through the ideal low-pass filter. Its cutoff is two thousand pi radians per second. The question wants the filter and output spectrum sketched in hertz, so let's convert the cutoff first.
$f_{\mathrm{cut}}=1000\ \mathrm{Hz}$
Divide two thousand pi by two pi. The passband is therefore between negative one thousand and positive one thousand hertz.
$[-500,500]\ \mathrm{Hz}\quad\mathrm{passes}$
The centered rectangle lies entirely inside the passband, because it ends at plus and minus five hundred hertz. The filter passes this baseband copy unchanged, including its height of pi over two.
$[1500,2500]\ \mathrm{Hz}\quad\mathrm{is\ rejected}$

The shifted right rectangle starts at fifteen hundred hertz, beyond the positive one-thousand-hertz cutoff. The left shifted rectangle is also outside the passband. Both shifted copies are removed completely.
$Z(\omega)=\frac12X(\omega)$
Only the centered half-amplitude spectrum survives. Therefore Z of omega equals one-half X of omega. This is the crucial filtering result, and it follows immediately from your drawing.
$z(t)=\frac12x(t)=\frac{\sin(1000\pi t)}{2t}$
Taking the inverse transform is now easy. Scaling a spectrum by one-half scales its time-domain signal by one-half. The output is the original input at half amplitude.
Interpretation: same waveform shape, half the amplitude.

The filter removes the high-frequency shifted copies, but keeps the central copy. That is why the recovered waveform has exactly the same shape and frequencies as the original, just scaled down. This is the physical point of the modulation-and-filtering problem.

title: 14B  CHECK THE OUTPUT SPECTRUM
topic: WHY THE DEMODULATED OUTPUT IS HALF SIZE
steps: $H(2\pi f)=1\ \mathrm{when}\ |f|<1000\ \mathrm{Hz}$
On the diagram, imagine two vertical filter boundaries at negative one thousand and positive one thousand hertz. Only the centered spectrum lies between those boundaries.
$Z(\omega)=\frac12X(\omega)$
The blue center rectangle passes with height pi over two. The two yellow sidebands are outside the passband and are discarded entirely. So Z equals one-half X.
$z(t)=\frac{\sin(1000\pi t)}{2t}$
Converting back to time is just a scaling operation now. The reconstructed signal is sine of one thousand pi t divided by two t, meaning the original signal at half amplitude.
Final check: same bandwidth, same shape.

The passband did not shrink the useful rectangle, so the recovered signal has exactly the same frequency content and time-domain shape as the original. Its only change is the one-half amplitude factor.

title: 15  EXAM STRATEGY: FOUR REUSABLE MOVES
steps: $\mathrm{sinusoid}\ \longrightarrow\ \mathrm{Euler\ pairs}$
First, when you see a sine or cosine inside a periodic-signal problem, expand it using Euler's identities. Match positive and negative harmonic frequencies separately, and check conjugate symmetry.
$\mathrm{delay}\ \longrightarrow\ \mathrm{phase\ only}$
Second, when you see a time delay, look for a complex exponential phase factor. Do not change the coefficient magnitudes or the frequency locations.
$\mathrm{ideal\ filter}\ \longrightarrow\ \mathrm{keep\ or\ delete}$
Third, for an ideal frequency filter, identify the spectral components that fall inside its passband and delete the rest. Then reconstruct the output signal from the surviving terms.
$\mathrm{time\ multiplication}\ \longrightarrow\ \mathrm{spectral\ shifts}$
Fourth, when a signal is multiplied by a cosine, anticipate shifted copies of its spectrum. For cosine squared, first use the power-reduction identity and track all three spectral pieces.
Pause here and redo each problem from a blank page.

The point of a good worked example is not to memorize my final line. It is to rebuild the reasoning independently. Try question two in the Fall twenty twenty six review first, followed by the filter question, and then the modulation question.
